hints.text: The likelihood of nine heads is 1 for the special coin and 1/512 for a fair coin.

solution.setup: Apply Bayes' rule to the special-coin and fair-coin hypotheses.
solution.reasoning: The posterior is (1/500)/[(1/500)+(499/500)(1/512)]. Multiplying numerator and denominator by 500·512 gives 512/(512+499).
solution.sanityCheck: Nine heads supply odds of 512:1, almost offsetting prior odds of 499:1 against the special coin.

keyInsight: Rare priors can be overcome when the evidence has a comparably large likelihood ratio.
recognitionCues: Repeated observations update a hidden-source hypothesis.
commonMistakes: Ignoring the 499 ordinary coins when applying Bayes' rule.
followUps: How many consecutive heads are needed for posterior probability above 90%?

source.notes: Original variant of a publicly reported interview family associated with Hudson River Trading, Jane Street.

title: Nine Heads From a Mystery Coin
problem: A box contains 500 coins: one is double-headed and 499 are fair. A coin is chosen uniformly and produces nine heads in nine flips. What is the probability it is the double-headed coin?
